fable-5.1.text:
I think that claim gets the direction of the effect roughly backwards, at least for now. What a coding agent is good at is the part of research that was never really the bottleneck. If I have a clear idea, writing the training script, setting up the data loader, running the sweep, making the plots, that was always the easy part. A good student could do it in a week; now the agent does it in an afternoon. That's real, and I don't want to downplay it. But it compresses execution, it doesn't compress the thing that actually makes a project succeed or fail, which is deciding what to try.

When I look back at the projects I'm most proud of, the hard part was almost never the implementation. With ConvNeXt, the code was trivial, it's a ResNet with a bunch of modifications. The hard part was the question: is the gap between ConvNets and Transformers about the architecture, or about the training recipe and a few design decisions that happened to accumulate in one camp? Once you ask that question the right way, the experiments are obvious. Same with the pruning work. The experiments were simple, the point was noticing that everyone was assuming the inherited weights mattered and nobody had checked. An agent will happily run whatever you tell it to run. It won't tell you that your question is wrong, or that the baseline everybody uses is secretly unfair.

So what I actually see happening is that the role of the student changes rather than disappears. The parts of a PhD that were apprenticeship in engineering shrink, and the parts that are apprenticeship in judgment become almost the whole thing. Which experiment is worth running, what result would actually surprise you, when to stop a direction, how to tell a clean finding from a lucky seed. Those are learned by doing lots of projects and being wrong a lot, with someone around to tell you why. I don't know how to teach that without a person going through it.

There's also a more practical worry. If a student uses an agent for everything from day one, they may never develop the intuition that comes from having debugged the thing yourself. When a training run diverges, I want a student who has a feeling for whether it's the learning rate, the data, or a shape bug, before they ask anyone or anything. That feeling comes from suffering through it a few times. So I actually tell my students to use these tools heavily, but to make sure they could have done it themselves, at least once.

And then honestly, the thing I keep coming back to is that research taste is partly a social process. Students bring in questions I wouldn't have asked, they push back, they get obsessed with something I think is a dead end and sometimes they're right. The agent is extremely capable and extremely agreeable. That second property is not what you want in a collaborator. So, unnecessary, no. Different, yes, and I think the students who figure out that their value is in the questions, not the code, will do much better than the ones who are competing with the agent at the thing the agent is already good at.

opus-5.5.text:
I don't really buy that claim, at least not in the strong form. Coding agents are clearly getting very good. In my own group I see students using them all the time to write training scripts, debug data loaders, set up baselines, and run ablations much faster than before. Some things that used to take a student a week now take an afternoon. That part is real, and I think it would be silly to pretend otherwise.

But I think the claim confuses what a research student actually does. Writing code was never the core of a PhD. It's the medium. The hard parts are deciding which question is worth asking, noticing that a result is weird and refusing to move on until you understand why, choosing the right experiment so that the outcome actually changes your belief, and having the taste to tell an interesting finding from an artifact. A lot of the papers I'm happiest with came from someone staring at a plot and saying, "wait, that shouldn't happen." The agents aren't very good at that kind of sustained curiosity and skepticism yet. They're very good at executing a well-specified plan. Research is mostly about figuring out the plan when nobody has specified it.

There's also the training aspect. A PhD isn't just labor for the advisor. It's how you produce the next generation of people who can do research independently. If you replaced students with agents, you might get some papers out faster for a few years, but you'd stop producing people who can define new directions. That would be a pretty bad trade for the field.

What I do think changes is the shape of the job. The bottleneck shifts away from implementation and toward ideas, judgment, and evaluation. A student with good agents can explore a much bigger space, maybe run ten variants instead of two, so the premium on asking good questions and designing clean experiments actually goes up. And there's a new skill: verifying what the agent did. It's easy to get a result that looks great because of a subtle bug or a leaked test set. So you need people who understand the system deeply enough to catch that.

So my view is that agents make research students more productive, and they raise the bar on what a good student looks like. I don't think they make students unnecessary. If anything, I'd tell students to lean into these tools heavily, but to invest even more in the things the tools don't give you: intuition, taste, and the habit of really understanding why something works.

fable-5.text:
I don't think that claim holds up, at least not in the way people usually frame it. What AI coding agents are really good at right now is executing well-specified tasks — you tell them "implement this baseline, run this ablation, make this plot," and they'll do it faster than a first-year student would. So if your mental model of a research student is "someone who writes code for the advisor's ideas," then yes, that role is getting automated, and honestly it should be.

But that was never the actual value of a research student. The value is in the parts that come before and after the code: noticing that an experiment result is weird in a way that suggests the problem is framed wrong, developing taste about which questions are worth asking, being the person who says "wait, our baseline is suspiciously strong, something's off in the data." In my experience, the hardest part of research is almost never the implementation — it's knowing what to try, and knowing when to stop trying something. Coding agents today don't have that judgment, and when they fail, they often fail confidently, which means you still need someone with enough understanding to audit the output.

There's also a training argument that I think people miss. The way students develop research taste is by going through the grind — implementing things, breaking them, debugging, and building intuition from that contact with reality. If agents take over all the low-level work, we have to be careful we're not removing the ladder that produces the next generation of people who can direct the agents. So the role changes, definitely. Students in my group now spend relatively more time on experimental design, on reading results critically, on verification. But "the role changes" is very different from "the role disappears." If anything, when execution gets cheap, the bottleneck shifts to having good ideas and good judgment — and that's exactly what we're supposed to be training students to develop.

opus-5.text:
I think the claim confuses research with implementation. If what a student contributed was typing out the training loop, then yes, that part is getting cheap fast. But in my experience that was never the bottleneck. The bottleneck is knowing which experiment is worth running, and then being honest about what the result actually says.

A lot of the work I'm proudest of is basically that. When we looked at network pruning, the finding was that the baselines people were comparing against were undertrained — you could match the fancy pruned model by just training a small network properly. With ConvNeXt, the question was whether transformers were winning because of attention or because of a pile of training recipe changes everyone had adopted along the way. Neither of those is a coding problem. An agent will happily implement whatever comparison you ask for, including the unfair one, and it'll produce a number with three decimal places that looks completely convincing.

So if anything, agents make taste more valuable, not less. When running an experiment costs you an afternoon instead of three weeks, you can run a hundred of them, and now your binding constraint is the ability to look at a hundred results and not fool yourself. That's a skill, and it's learned slowly, mostly by being wrong in front of someone who points it out.

The other thing I'd say is that a university isn't a paper factory. Training people who can think carefully about evidence is the output, not a cost of producing the output. Even if an agent could write my next paper, I'd still want the students.

sonnet-5.5.text:
I think it's an overstatement, though there's something real behind it. Coding agents have changed a lot of what a research student spends time on. Implementing a baseline, writing an evaluation script, or running a sweep used to take days, and now it often takes hours. That part of the job is getting automated, and I'd be lying if I said it wasn't affecting how we work.

But I don't think writing code was ever the core of research. The hard parts are deciding which question is worth asking, noticing that a result looks strange and deserves a closer look, designing the experiment that separates two hypotheses, and knowing when a number is too good to be true. Agents are much better at executing a well-specified task than at deciding what the task should be. When the specification is vague, or when the interesting thing is something nobody has thought to look for, you still need a person with taste and context.

There's also a training issue. Students become good researchers partly by going through the details themselves: debugging a training run that silently diverges, finding a bug in the data pipeline, or realizing the baseline wasn't tuned properly. If you hand all of that off, you may never build the intuition to tell whether the agent's output is right. Someone has to verify the work, and verification needs expertise.

So I'd say the role is shifting, not disappearing. Students can try more ideas and operate at a higher level, closer to directing a small team of fast but sometimes careless collaborators. The students who do well will be the ones who ask good questions and are skeptical of results. If anything, that raises the bar for what a good research student looks like. And I'm not sure the tools can do the whole thing yet, especially the part where you decide what's interesting.

haiku-5.5.text:
I think the claim gets part of it right. Coding agents are now good at the mechanical parts of research: writing training loops, wiring up evaluation scripts, chasing down a bug in a data loader. That's real leverage. But the bottleneck in a research project has rarely been typing speed. It's deciding which question is worth asking, noticing when a result is an artifact, and knowing which of a dozen plausible explanations to chase. Those are judgment skills, and people usually build them by doing the messy work themselves, which is exactly the part that's now easy to skip.

So I don't think students become unnecessary. The risk is that they produce a lot of output without developing the taste that makes the output mean something. If an agent wrote the code, you should still be able to explain each choice in it and predict what it will do before you run it. If you can't, you don't yet understand your own experiment.

I think the role shifts more than it disappears. Advisors will probably expect more independent scoping and more rigorous ablations, since trying things is cheaper now. A student who can use agents to test ten hypotheses in a day, then reason carefully about which two matter, is more valuable than one who implements the single idea they were handed. Whether we train people to do that well is the open question.

astra-6.text:
I think that’s a very narrow view of what research students do. Coding is one part of research, and if an agent can help you implement an idea faster, that’s great. But a lot of the difficulty is figuring out which question is worth asking, designing an experiment that actually answers it, and understanding what happened when the result is unexpected.

Often you don’t have a clear specification. You try something, discover that your assumption was wrong, and change direction. Better coding tools can make that process faster, but you still need scientific judgment.

And students are developing that judgment through doing research. I would be careful about removing all the hands-on work, because debugging an implementation can be where you realize you didn’t really understand the idea. So I see an opportunity to help students become more capable and ambitious. I don’t see faster code generation as a reason to conclude that we no longer need them.

sol-6.1.text:
I don’t agree with that. I think it comes from a very narrow view of what a research student does. If you think their job is just to take a specification and write the code, then, sure, a coding agent could do more and more of that. But in research, figuring out the specification is often the hard part. What question should we ask? What experiment would actually tell us something? When we get a surprising result, is it a bug, or is there an interesting idea there?

And students are developing that judgment through doing the work. Even an experiment that fails can be valuable if you understand why it failed. So I would hope these tools help students explore more ideas and spend more time thinking deeply. I don’t see faster coding as a reason to stop training researchers. It gives us an opportunity to change how we train them.
